content: The National Library of Medicine needs a digital repository for collection materials produced by existing and future digitization projects. Members of the public and NIH staff should be able to discover and view permitted materials, while authorized library staff need to create and maintain metadata, ingest or update digital objects, and manage their long-term preservation. Access may vary according to rights and user circumstances.

It should be the central home for digitized NLM collections, both for materials we already have and for new projects going forward. Right now, I see it supporting public and NIH access to approved content, while giving staff a reliable place to ingest, describe, and preserve objects. Over time, I’d want it to be the system that can handle new formats, new digitization workflows, and changing access rules without us having to rebuild everything.

For staff work, it needs to feel responsive enough that people can search, review records, and ingest content without long delays, but I don’t have exact timing targets yet. For the public, we’d expect normal web-app performance even as the collection grows a lot over time, since the repository could end up serving a very large amount of content and more users than we have today. Uptime should be high because this is a core access point for both internal and public use, but I’d need to confirm the specific availability expectations with the team.

Yes, we’d want it to handle heavier public use gracefully during announcements, discovery spikes, or when a popular collection gets attention. NIH and library staff would likely have more predictable workday usage, but they still need reliable access for ingest, metadata updates, and preservation tasks, so disruptions there are a real problem. I’d also want it to tolerate brief outages or maintenance windows without losing work or causing access problems once service comes back, though the exact recovery expectations would need to be confirmed.

A good experience means people can search or browse, understand what they’re looking at, and get to the item or metadata they need without having to ask for help. For the public, that mostly means clear labels, straightforward navigation, and obvious access restrictions when something can’t be viewed. For staff, it needs to be efficient and consistent enough that they can do routine work quickly without a lot of training or workarounds.

It needs to respect rights restrictions very carefully, so not every user will be able to see every object or every piece of metadata. We also have to protect staff accounts and any sensitive administrative information, and comply with federal expectations around records handling, accessibility, and preservation. In practice, that means access has to be role-based and sometimes item-specific, with controls that make it clear what can be viewed, downloaded, or edited by each type of user.

I don’t know that we’ve finalized the exact role map yet. In general, I’d expect a smaller set of authorized staff to create and edit metadata, a more restricted group to approve or publish records, and preservation or system staff to have broader technical access without necessarily being able to change descriptive data. We’d need to verify the specific separation of duties with the library team before locking that down.

They should be blocked cleanly and told, in plain language, that they don’t have permission for that action. For public users, that might mean they can see basic descriptive information but not the file itself, while staff might be able to view a record but not edit or publish it. We’d also want the system to avoid exposing hidden details in error messages, and if possible guide the user to the right next step, like requesting access or contacting the appropriate staff group.

For the public, the message should be simple and non-technical, like that the item isn’t available to view or download due to rights or access restrictions. If there’s a legitimate path to request access, it should point them to that, but otherwise it can just explain that the content is restricted. For library staff, the message should be a little more specific and direct them to the correct internal contact or workflow when their role doesn’t allow the action, without revealing anything sensitive about the item itself.

It should block the action, and it should direct them to the appropriate internal support or system owner if there’s a legitimate need. We wouldn’t want staff guessing or trying workarounds, so the message should point them to the correct team or process for access requests or role changes. At the same time, it should keep administrative details private and not say more than necessary about what they were trying to reach.

We’d need the system to support rights holders being either internal NLM staff or an external copyright or permissions holder, depending on the item. In some cases the approval source might be a specific project owner or a designated rights contact rather than the original creator. I don’t know that we’ve defined every category yet, but the repository should be flexible enough to record who granted the permission and under what basis.

We’d want to use established authority sources wherever possible, especially for names, subjects, and other core descriptive fields, so records are consistent and searchable. I’m not sure we’ve picked the exact vocabularies yet, but the expectation is to align with library and archival standards rather than invent our own terms. For special cases, like an unusual format, a project-specific note, or something not covered by the authority source, staff may need to enter a controlled local value or free text, but that should be the exception rather than the rule.

Yes, for some fields we’d want the system to recognize more than one approved source rather than forcing a single one. For example, names might come from an established name authority, subjects from a subject heading source, and genres or forms from a separate controlled list, depending on the collection. I don’t know that we’ve locked the exact approved sources yet, so the repository should probably allow configuration by field and collection, with staff choosing among the approved options where that makes sense.

They should capture enough to show who authorized it, what exactly was authorized, and when it happened. At minimum I’d expect the approver’s identity or role, the type of permission granted, and the date of approval, and if there’s documentation or a citation behind it, that should be linked or noted too. We may not need every case to have the same level of detail, but the record should be strong enough that someone can later understand why the item was made available.

Staff should be guided by the collection or item type, and the system should make the preferred source clear in the metadata form or workflow. If there are multiple approved sources for a field, we’d want one to be primary by default, with the others available only when the primary source doesn’t fit or doesn’t have the needed term. Any collection-specific exceptions should be handled by configuration or guidance from the managing staff, because that kind of rule will vary across projects.

The main outcomes are making permitted materials easy to discover and view, getting new digitized content into the repository accurately, and preserving the digital objects over the long term. We also need staff to be able to maintain metadata and manage rights correctly, because access and preservation both depend on that. If there’s a conflict, I’d say rights compliance and preservation integrity come first, then accurate ingest and metadata, and then discovery convenience, because we can’t expose or manage content properly if the rights or preservation side is wrong.

Yes, I would expect some nice-to-have discovery features to be deferred if they don’t affect basic access or preservation, like advanced browse facets, richer public display options, or more elaborate analytics. We’d also be open to postponing automation that’s useful but not essential, such as highly sophisticated metadata suggestions, as long as staff can still complete ingest and rights management manually. Anything that affects compliance, preservation, or core public access would be much harder to defer.

We should capture acceptance criteria around successful ingest, metadata creation and update, rights-based access control, public discovery of permitted items, and preservation actions like fixity and storage validation. I’d also want clear criteria for staff workflows, such as whether authorized users can complete their tasks without workarounds and whether the system reliably reflects access restrictions. The biggest unresolved questions are probably the exact approval sources, the detailed rights logic for different user groups, and which collection-specific metadata rules still need to be finalized.

The biggest conflicts will probably be between broad public access and strict rights restrictions, and between collection-specific metadata practices and having a consistent repository-wide workflow. We’ll also run into tradeoffs when a collection wants more detailed description but staff need a faster ingest process, or when preservation wants to keep everything while access rules say only some items can be visible. I’d handle those by making rights and compliance the deciding factor, then using configurable collection rules and documented exceptions so we can be consistent without blocking legitimate collection needs.

Staff should follow the standard process unless there is a documented, approved exception that applies to that specific collection or item. The exception should be tied to a named authority, be current, and be visible in the record so staff can justify why they did not use the default rule. If there’s any doubt, the default should win until a manager or rights authority confirms the exception.

If the rights status is unclear, the safest rule is to restrict public access until the status is verified by the authorized staff. If the item has mixed rights, then the most restrictive applicable rule should govern what the public can see, while staff may still have broader internal access if that’s allowed. When rights change later, the repository should be updated as quickly as practical by staff, with the expectation that public discovery and the access setting change together so they stay in sync.

A readiness check should confirm that authorized staff can create and edit metadata, ingest or update objects, and assign rights or access settings without needing manual data fixes outside the system. It should also show that access rules are enforced consistently for public users, NIH staff, and repository staff, including cases with restricted, mixed, or unpublished materials. I’d want test cases proving that the same item appears differently depending on user role and rights status, and that those results stay correct after updates, so we know the system behaves reliably in normal day-to-day use.

Anonymous users should be able to search and view only the materials that are explicitly permitted for public access. An authenticated user, such as NIH staff, may be allowed to see additional materials if their role or permissions permit it, but that still depends on the rights attached to the item. Anything restricted should be blocked for anonymous users, and if an item is not cleared for public viewing, they should not get past the access control step.

Public search and viewing should stay available during spikes as long as the system can safely support it, because public access is part of the mission. If we need throttling for stability, I’d expect it to protect the system first and to favor authenticated staff for administrative functions, while keeping public discovery and viewing as available as possible. I don’t think we’ve decided the exact priority or rate-limiting rules yet, so that would need to be defined with the technical team and leadership.

If the site is under normal load, public search and viewing should continue normally. If performance degrades, public discovery should still be available but may be slowed or queued before anything that affects staff administration, and we should avoid blocking access to already permitted public materials unless there is no other option. Staff-only actions like ingest, metadata correction, rights updates, and preservation workflows should take priority so the repository can stay accurate and operational.

The repository should handle the core preservation basics internally, including storing fixity information, running routine checksum or fixity checks, and flagging any corruption or change. It should also support planned format migration or at least preserve enough metadata and derivation history so we can manage migrations over time without losing provenance. For obsolete file types, I’d expect the system to retain the original bitstream if policy allows, while also providing a usable access copy or a clear path for staff to create one.

The authoritative decision-maker should be designated library staff, likely within the digital collections or rights management side, rather than the system making that judgment on its own. If different user groups or collection rules conflict, the repository should apply the most restrictive valid rule until staff resolve the conflict and record the final rights decision. I don’t think the exact approval chain is settled yet, so we’d need to confirm which staff role has final authority and whether there are any exceptions for NIH or legal review.

In that case, the repository should keep the preserved content safe but not expose it publicly until the rights decision is final. Ideally it would show only a minimal restricted representation, like a metadata record or placeholder, if staff want the item discoverable without revealing the content itself. If even that is too risky, then it should be hidden from general users and only visible to authorized staff until the matter is resolved.

Yes, staff should be able to review the original preserved bitstream, edit the placeholder or restricted metadata, and update the rights decision when it changes. They should also be able to trigger a release or make the item public once the review is complete and the object is cleared for access. For auditability, those actions should be tracked so we know who changed what and when.

We should keep version history for meaningful changes, especially anything affecting the content, rights, or preservation copy. I wouldn’t want routine metadata fixes to create a new formal version every time, but the system should still audit those changes. For prior content versions, the default should be to retain them as long as policy allows, since provenance and preservation history matter, but I suspect there may be retention rules we’d need to confirm with records and legal staff.

If the preservation copy itself changes, that should create a new formal version. If only routine metadata changes, then an audit trail is enough, unless the metadata change affects access, rights, or descriptive identity in a meaningful way, in which case I’d expect both a version note and an audit record. If both happen together, the repository should do both so the preservation history stays clear and the administrative history is complete.

The practical rule should be that staff update the repository as soon as the rights decision is confirmed, with the expectation that access changes take effect immediately or within the same business day. I do think there can be cases where public discovery and the access setting do not change at exactly the same time, especially if we want to keep a record visible as a placeholder while the content itself remains restricted. In those cases, the metadata record could stay discoverable while the actual access permission is held back until the final release decision.

The final say should rest with the designated rights authority in the library, probably the staff member or team responsible for digital collections rights decisions. Other staff roles like cataloging, preservation, or project staff should review and recommend, but not override the final call unless there’s a compliance or legal concern that escalates it. If there is a dispute, I’d expect it to go to a higher-level library manager or legal/privacy review before access is granted or withheld.

In-progress staff work should ideally resume automatically if the system can safely pick up where it left off, especially for things like batch ingest, metadata edits, or queued preservation actions. If an operation was interrupted in a way that leaves uncertainty, then staff should have to restart or confirm it rather than the system guessing. For user requests, I’d expect them to stay queued or get a clear failure message so they can retry once service is back.

If the request is safe to retry without duplicating anything or changing the outcome, it should stay queued for automatic completion. If there’s any risk of duplicate ingest, duplicate notification, or an access decision being applied twice, it should be marked failed and left for manual retry. I’d especially treat rights-related changes and preservation writes more cautiously than simple viewing or download requests.

Yes, in the first release I would want basic validation, duplicate detection, and clear status tracking to be built in because staff need those to safely complete ingest and updates. I’d also want some kind of automatic rights flagging or access check so staff aren’t manually guessing before something is exposed. More advanced discovery features, like richer search facets or recommendation-style browsing, can wait if needed as long as the core ingest, rights, and preservation tasks are reliable.

In practice, the system should alert staff right away and block public access until the issue is reviewed. If the object is confirmed corrupted or altered, I’d expect it to be quarantined and marked for remediation, with controlled replacement allowed only by authorized staff and only if we have a trusted replacement copy. The response could differ if the item is known to be a working or derivative copy, but for preservation masters I’d want a much stricter default.

Yes, definitely. Public anonymous requests can usually be retried automatically if they’re simple read-only actions like viewing a permitted item, because there’s little risk in trying again. Staff actions, especially anything that changes metadata, rights, or preservation content, should be treated more cautiously and usually need manual confirmation if they were interrupted.

I’d support richer item presentation now if it directly helps users understand what they’re looking at, like thumbnails, page images, or basic descriptive context. Advanced browse facets and usage analytics could be deferred if needed, because they’re helpful but not essential to the core repository function. The one exception is if a particular collection has a public-facing access need that depends on a specific browse path or presentation feature, then that feature becomes a must-have for that collection.

Download and reuse should follow the rights status of the item, so if something is open it can be downloaded, but if rights are restricted the system should limit copying or hide the download option. Role matters too, because NIH staff may need broader access than the general public for some internal or restricted collections. I’d also expect collection-specific conditions to override the general rule when there are donor restrictions, privacy concerns, or other special handling requirements.
